name: Saint Bernard of Clairvaux
history: A young Burgundian noble who entered the struggling monastery of Cîteaux with about thirty relatives and friends, then became founding abbot of Clairvaux. Bernard was the most influential churchman of his age, a mystic, preacher and counsellor of popes. His sermons on the Song of Songs and on Our Lady earned him the title of the honey-sweet doctor.
life: Bernard arrived at Cîteaux in 1113, and his coming revived the new Cistercian reform. In 1115 he was sent to found Clairvaux, and from there some seventy monasteries were founded in his lifetime. He was drawn constantly into the affairs of the Church: he helped end the schism of 1130 on the side of Innocent II, advised his former monk, Pope Eugene III, and argued against Peter Abelard. At the pope’s request he preached the Second Crusade, whose failure grieved him deeply. When a wandering monk stirred up attacks on the Jews of the Rhineland, Bernard went there in person and stopped him. Yet his heart was in the cloister. He wrote of the love of God, of humility and of the Virgin Mary with great warmth, and Dante chose him as his last guide in Paradise. He died in 1153 and was named a Doctor of the Church in 1830.
prayerTo: Saint Bernard, you loved Christ with all your heart and taught the Church to look to Mary in every danger. Pray that in temptation and confusion I may look to the star and call upon her. Help me to love God for His own sake, and to love Him without measure. Amen.
penance: Pray the Memorare slowly today, or a decade of the Rosary, for someone who has lost hope.
meditation: In dangers, in difficulties, in doubts, think of Mary, call upon Mary, Bernard preached. What doubt or difficulty will you bring to her today?
prayer: O God, who didst give blessed Bernard to be thy people’s minister in eternal salvation; grant, we pray, that we who have him for teacher of life here on earth, may also deserve now that he is in heaven, to have him for an advocate. Through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
prayerSource: Collect of the day, Roman Missal of 1962
